sections.h2: Selling a house in Sahuarita, AZ
sections.html:
Sahuarita homeowners can use an agent, sell on their own, or take an offer from a cash buyer with no mortgage. The right pick depends on how soon you need to close and how much work the house needs. This is a town of family homes, with 81.0 percent of occupied homes lived in by their owners.

  • Agent listing: you prepare the house, allow showings and wait for the buyer's loan to clear.
  • Sale by owner: you set the price, meet buyers and prepare the deed and affidavit yourself.
  • Cash sale: no bank is involved, and you weigh the offer against the net from a listing after repairs and fees.

Get the terms in writing whichever way you go, and check the permit points below before you sign.

Sahuarita is in Pima County, about 15 miles south of Tucson. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 37,694 residents, 10.6 percent above the 2020 base. The median owner-occupied home was valued at $364,300 for 2020 to 2024, median gross rent was $1,837 and median household income was $104,680. Households average 2.89 people.

A median describes the whole town, so use it only as a rough check on an offer. The mean commute is 28.6 minutes, and the Sun Shuttle serves Sahuarita and Tucson on weekdays only, so a buyer who works in Tucson will weigh the drive.

Buyers often ask about the planned communities, because their rules and fees differ from an ordinary subdivision. Rancho Sahuarita and its resort sit in the north, Quail Creek in the southeast and Madera Highlands in the south. If your house is in one, ask the association for its governing documents and a statement of dues. The buyer will want both during escrow.

Most of the town is in Sahuarita Unified School District, and a portion is in the Continental Elementary School District. Boundaries do not follow the town line, so ask the district to confirm the assigned schools for your exact address. Families check this early, so put the district in your listing or offer packet.

Unpermitted work and open complaints are the two things most likely to surface in an inspection. The Community Development Department handles building and zoning compliance. Weeds, junk vehicles and illegal signs go to Planning and Zoning. A structure built without a permit, or a substandard or dangerous one, goes to Building Safety. Complaints can be filed through the Accela Citizen Access portal, in person, or by phone at (520) 822-8852.

Most alterations, replacements and repairs need a permit. A few small items do not:

ProjectExempt from a building permit up to
One-story detached shed200 square feet, with no plumbing, electrical or mechanical work
Masonry wall6 feet high
Wood, vinyl or wrought iron fence7 feet high
Retaining wall4 feet high
Deck not attached to the house200 square feet and no more than 30 inches above grade

Private concrete paths and driveways, painting, tile, carpet and cabinet replacement are also exempt. A room addition, a patio enclosure or new wiring belongs with the Building Safety Division at 520-822-8866. If you added something without a permit, call before you list and decide whether to permit it or disclose it and sell as is.

sections.h2: What to do about unpermitted work
sections.html:
Most buyers do not mind a shed or a fence. They mind surprises. If you built something that needed a permit and never got one, you have two choices. You can ask Building Safety what it would take to permit the work now, or you can disclose it and sell the house as is, which usually lowers a buyer's offer or points the deal toward a cash purchase.

Take photos of the work, find any receipts from the contractor and write down the year it was done. If the work involved wiring or plumbing, say so, because buyers and inspectors treat those differently from a painted fence. A short, honest summary handed over early builds more trust than a clever explanation given late.

Open complaints matter too. If a neighbor reported weeds, a junk vehicle or a sign, clear the problem first and keep proof of the fix. The Community Development Department can tell you whether a complaint is still open on your address.

An association adds a step to every sale. Contact its manager as soon as you decide to sell and ask for the governing documents and a statement of any dues owed. A balance left unpaid has to be settled at closing, and it can hold up the deed if nobody knows the figure in time.

Ask whether the association restricts rentals, fences, sheds or exterior changes, since a buyer will ask and the answer can move the price. Keep the paperwork in the same folder as your tax bill and deed so the title company can pick it up in one place.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Pima County
sections.html:
The Pima County Recorder charges a flat $30 to record any document under A.R.S. 11-475. A document returned after being submitted in error costs $5, and mailed documents carry a $1 processing fee. Cash, checks and money orders are accepted, and Visa and Mastercard work for in-person payments only. The affidavit of property value form comes from the Arizona Department of Revenue.

A deed that transfers title needs that affidavit under A.R.S. 11-1133, signed by buyer and seller or their agents. It asks for the price, the parcel number and the date of sale. Without a complete affidavit or an exemption notation, the recorder must refuse the deed. Ask the Pima County Treasurer for your current tax bill, since the closing figures depend on it.

1. Decide on a route and ask for offers in writing.
  2. Get HOA documents and a dues statement if you are in a planned community.
  3. Call the Building Safety Division about any work done without a permit.
  4. Pull your tax bill from the Treasurer.
  5. Open escrow so the title company can prepare the deed and affidavit.
  6. The deed is recorded with the Pima County Recorder and your proceeds follow.

A cash sale cuts out the buyer's loan approval, though it does not remove the permit questions, the HOA package or recording.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Pima County?
faqs.a: A flat $30 per document. Mailed documents add a $1 processing fee, and the affidavit of property value form comes from the Arizona Department of Revenue.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a shed or fence in Sahuarita?
faqs.a: Not always. A one-story detached shed up to 200 square feet with no utilities, masonry walls up to 6 feet and fences up to 7 feet are exempt from a building permit. Anything larger, or with plumbing or electrical work, needs one.
Most of the town is in Sahuarita Unified School District, with a portion in the Continental Elementary School District. Confirm the assignment for your address with the district.

faqs.q: How many people live in Sahuarita?
faqs.a: An estimated 37,694 as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 34,134 and the 2010 census counted 25,259.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a code complaint in Sahuarita?
faqs.a: The Community Development Department at (520) 822-8852, or file online through Accela Citizen Access. For permit questions, the Building Safety Division is at 520-822-8866.
